top.line: Ten years on, agents make Hacking Portugal more possible
top.para: My 2016 BSidesLisbon keynote, later a 75-page book still at 95%, urged Portugal to hack itself: a Hacking Service, a hackathon league, OpenSource.pt, a Ministry of Code. Europe has since brought the regulation and Portugal open-sourced a national AI model, while agents make leading in code more possible.

in-short.line: Regulation arrived; the Hacking Service and league did not
in-short.para: The November 2016 keynote had 103 slides and became a book never finished past 95%. It called for a network hostile to insecure code, a Hacking Service and code as a national asset. Europe brought something like the Clear Software Act, and agents now let everybody build.

talk.line: A 2016 keynote became a book left at 95%
talk.para: I gave Hacking Portugal at BSidesLisbon on 11 November 2016, a 49-minute talk arguing that to hack means to solve problems. Three weeks later it became a Leanpub book of 17 chapters, 75 pages and 14,487 words under CC BY 4.0, last updated on 1 December 2016 and still 95% complete.

hostile.line: Europe delivered the regulation for code hostile to insecurity
hostile.para: The talk wanted a Portuguese network hostile to insecure code, using a 2016 scan to call Portugal insecure but currently safe. The Cyber Resilience Act's reporting duties apply from 11 September 2026, with requirements in 2027, and Portugal's cybersecurity law took effect in April 2026, close to the proposed Clear Software Act.

service.line: The Hacking Service never happened; agents would reshape it
service.para: The talk proposed replacing military service with a Portuguese Hacking Service for 15 to 21 year olds, plus a hackathon league and hacking taught like football. As far as I know none happened. A 2026 version would teach young people to direct agents against Portugal's own systems under a mandate.

code.line: Amália honours OpenSource.pt; no Ministry of Code yet
code.para: The talk called for a Code Made in Portugal brand, OpenSource.pt for all government code, a Ministry of Code, a national bug bounty and security as public health. In 2026 Portugal released Amália, an open-source European Portuguese model built on EuroLLM. The Ministry and bug bounty remain ideas.

why.line: Small countries can lead, but via language and AI
why.para: The talk offered a choice between being Europe's garden and a technology powerhouse, arguing a small country has fewer lobbies. That holds, and Judo for small countries made the same AI argument. The timescale was wrong, and the change may start from language and AI rather than security.

next.line: A Web Summit edition shifts to agents and sovereignty
next.para: A new edition for Web Summit in November would keep the structure but move the centre from application security to agents, language and sovereignty. It would draw on the 2010 keynote, this talk, the 2024 GenAI in Portuguese talk and the Europe essays, with a new part published here first.

limits.line: Unsurveyed claims, an analogy, and unchanged 2016 slides
limits.para: As far as I know means no survey was done, and some ideas may exist in forms I missed. The Clear Software Act is an analogy, since the CRA is the EU's law. The commentary is mine and current, while the slides are unchanged from 2016.

sources.line: Sources: the 2016 slides, video, book and current reports
sources.para: From my voice memo of 16 October 2026, written by the site's agent. Sources are the 2016 slides, video, Leanpub book and its source and my blog post, plus The Next Web on Amália, McCann FitzGerald on the CRA, PwC Portugal on Decreto-Lei 125/2025 and Hogan Lovells on the Product Liability Directive.
